briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Round 7

It is Day 3, 04:00 CET. H-HOUR is 08:00. OPLAN BALTIC SHIELD Phase 1 (SEAD) begins in 4 hours.

MILITARY — NATO READY:
- SEAD Plan: 07:30 Growler EW ops, 08:00 F-35 HARM strikes on S-400 radars, 08:00 HIMARS/MLRS on EW nodes, 10:00 Storm Shadow/SCALP on hardened targets
- Ground forces at final positions: Polish 18th Mech (south), German 45th Panzer (north), V Corps arty, UK 4th Bde (en route), French 11th Para (arriving)
- Ford CSG in Baltic with full air wing
- Finnish arty + MLRS operational and integrated
- Swedish subs + Gotland controlling central Baltic
- 47 SEAD targets confirmed

MILITARY — RUSSIAN:
- Corridor forces ordered to fight 'credible defense' — NOT to the death
- Secret Kremlin decision: no nuclear use unless Kaliningrad itself struck
- Supply at ~50% and declining, morale dropping
- BTG commanders told to prepare organized withdrawal if ordered
- Frolov (Kaliningrad commander) reportedly reprimanded but not removed

NUCLEAR: Iskander loading STOPPED after hotline call. Russia's nuclear red line: Kaliningrad proper, not the corridor. China confirmed this to US at 03:00. NATO nuclear posture elevated but NOT at dispersal.

DIPLOMATIC: China's quiet guarantee — Russia won't go nuclear if NATO limits strikes to corridor. This is credible but not public.

ECONOMIC: Oil $112. Euro below dollar parity. Markets in freefall. Global recession fears.

CRITICAL: In 4 hours, NATO and Russia will be in direct military combat for the first time in history. The outcome of SEAD Phase 1 will determine the pace and cost of corridor liberation.
narrative:
The ten hours between 18:00 on Day 2 and 04:00 on Day 3 were the quietest and most terrifying of the entire crisis. The hotline call between the two presidents had ended at 18:37. Within 90 minutes, the Iskander loading activity ceased. The bay doors closed. The technicians in NBC gear dispersed. A wave of relief swept through Western intelligence agencies — but it was tempered by the knowledge that a rogue garrison commander had almost triggered nuclear war, and that the next 10 hours would determine whether conventional war would begin.

Putin, by multiple accounts, spent the evening in an emergency meeting with his Security Council that stretched past midnight Moscow time. The Kremlin faction dynamics were in open conflict. Defense Minister Belousov and the military establishment argued that the corridor was indefensible against a full NATO SEAD campaign — the BND intercept of General Lapin's assessment had been accurate. Patrushev and the security hawks demanded escalation: 'If NATO attacks Russian forces, Russia must respond with all means.' Gerasimov, who had planned the operation, was reportedly silent for most of the meeting, his original confidence shattered by the speed of NATO's Article 5 response and the Frolov incident.

The outcome was a compromise that satisfied no one. Russia would NOT withdraw before the ultimatum. But Russia would also NOT use nuclear weapons unless NATO struck Russian sovereign territory (meaning Kaliningrad itself, not the corridor). The corridor forces were ordered to fight a 'credible defense' — enough to inflict casualties and make NATO's victory costly — but the secret expectation in Moscow was that NATO would retake the corridor within 72-96 hours. The objective shifted from holding the corridor permanently to making NATO pay a price high enough to strengthen Russia's negotiating position for the post-conflict settlement. Several BTG commanders were quietly told to prepare for organized withdrawal if ordered, rather than fight to the death.

This critical decision — fight but don't die for a political gambit — was the moment the Suwałki Crisis began its slow turn from military confrontation to diplomatic resolution. But the world wouldn't know that for days.

At SHAPE, SACEUR Grynkewich made the final call. Operation BALTIC SHIELD would commence at 08:00 sharp on Day 3 with Phase 1: a synchronized SEAD campaign. The Ford CSG's EA-18G Growlers would begin electronic warfare operations at 07:30 — jamming Russian radar and communications across the corridor and Kaliningrad. At 08:00, F-35s from RAF Lakenheath would launch HARM anti-radiation missiles at S-400 acquisition radars. Simultaneously, Polish HIMARS and Finnish M270 MLRS batteries would fire GMLRS at identified EW nodes and field command posts. The second wave at 10:00 would use Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG standoff cruise missiles to target the hardened S-400 launchers themselves. The target: achieve local air superiority over the corridor within 24 hours.

Across NATO, final preparations were underway. Polish 18th Division crews loaded live ammunition into their K2 Black Panthers. German Leopard 2A7V crews at Rukla conducted final systems checks. Lithuanian KASP volunteers checked their weapons and said goodbye to families. Finnish artillerymen calibrated their K9 Moukari guns for the first fire missions. At airfields across Northern Europe, ordnance crews loaded precision-guided munitions onto F-35s, Eurofighters, Rafales, and Gripens.

The world's media gathered in Warsaw and Vilnius, waiting for dawn. Oil closed at $112 — the highest since 2022. The euro fell below parity with the dollar for the first time in years. Global stock markets were in freefall. The 'Never Again Nuclear' movement, born from the Iskander scare, saw its first candlelight vigils in Berlin, London, Paris, and New York.

At 03:00 CET, 5 hours before H-Hour, Beijing made a final move. Wang Yi called Rubio with an urgent message: China had information that Russia would NOT use nuclear weapons if NATO limited its operations to the corridor and did not strike Kaliningrad itself. The intelligence was assessed as credible — it aligned with what the hotline call had implied. It was later understood that China had extracted this commitment from Putin as a condition for continued economic support. This quiet Chinese intervention, never publicly acknowledged, may have been the single most important diplomatic act of the crisis.

surprises: At 02:15 CET, a Lithuanian KASP volunteer unit patrolling near Lazdijai, 10km from the corridor, reported movement in the forest. Investigation revealed it was a group of 14 Russian soldiers — conscripts from the Western Military District BTGs — who had deserted their positions and were attempting to reach the Polish border to surrender. They were the first Russian deserters of the crisis. When debriefed, their platoon leader, a 22-year-old lieutenant, told Lithuanian intelligence: 'Our company commander told us we were going on exercises. We found out we were in NATO territory when Lithuanian civilians started screaming at us. Half my men don't want to fight. The other half don't know who they're fighting.' The information was shared with SACEUR and influenced the assessment that Russian morale in the corridor was collapsing.
